# Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience

Yuval Shalev Affiliation: University of Cambridge
Email: [ys716@cam.ac.uk](mailto:)    Zifeng Ding Affiliation: University
of Cambridge Email: [zd320@cam.ac.uk](mailto:)    Mateja Jamnik
Affiliation: University of Cambridge Email: [mj201@cam.ac.uk](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Language agents can adapt from experience in interactive environments,
but current reflection-based methods can only self-correct within a
single task instance. Whether such experience can be distilled into
reusable lessons that improve performance on future unseen tasks remains
unclear. We address this problem by introducing the In-context Training
(ICT) task, a framework for evaluating cross-task self-improvement in
language agents. In ICT, a reflector model observes trajectories
collected by an actor model and generates system prompts intended to
improve the actor’s performance on future unseen tasks. We then propose
an RL-based training pipeline for learning such reflections directly
from experience, without human-provided examples. Across ALFWorld and
MiniHack, our trained reflectors outperform an untrained baseline on
most held-out task families, showing that the ability to learn from
experience can itself be learned. In some cases, we observe
generalisation beyond the benchmark on which the reflector was trained,
to substantially different environments. Finally, we introduce MetaGym,
a generic Python library for constructing meta-environments, enabling
future research on self-improving language agents.

## 1 Introduction

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in using large
language models (LLMs) as decision-making agents in interactive
environments \[[18](#bib.bib9), [17](#bib.bib10)\]. In this setting,
LLMs act as agents that leverage their language capabilities to interact
with external environments, producing tokens that are interpreted as
actions \[[21](#bib.bib8)\]. When faced with an unfamiliar environment,
a general-purpose agent should be able to learn and adapt its behaviour
from experience in order to find an optimal policy for
action \[[16](#bib.bib7), [11](#bib.bib1), [23](#bib.bib6),
[14](#bib.bib4)\]. Humans handle this task with ease. For example, when
playing chess for the first time, a person may begin with an initial
strategy in mind and, after each game, reflect on their experience to
refine that strategy for future matches.

In LLM-based agents, the agent’s policy is determined not only by the
model’s parameters, but also by the prompt provided to the model, which
specifies how the agent should act in the environment \[[21](#bib.bib8),
[3](#bib.bib11)\]. Learning and adapting may therefore be achieved by
modifying the prompt provided to the model, making prompt optimisation a
natural mechanism for self-learning in language agents. This approach
has three main advantages: (1) it avoids the compute-heavy pipeline of
fine-tuning LLMs for each specific task through gradient descent; (2) it
leverages the linguistic abilities of the model to support rapid
learning from only a small number of experiences; and (3) it offers a
degree of transparency, since the accumulated experience is represented
solely in natural language and can be directly inspected.

Recent studies have explored self-improvement in language agents through
autonomous prompt modification, using self-reflection
mechanisms \[[14](#bib.bib4), [22](#bib.bib12), [5](#bib.bib13),
[6](#bib.bib14), [7](#bib.bib15)\]. In this setting, an LLM generates a
reflection following an unsuccessful attempt at an interactive task. The
reflection considers both the agent’s actions and the resulting feedback
from the environment, and is then used to guide the agent’s next attempt
by providing hints and suggesting how to avoid similar mistakes. This
yields a continuous online-learning mechanism, in which each task
attempt provides an additional data point for improving behaviour after
only a small number of trials.

However, existing work primarily focuses on self-correction by
repeatedly attempting the same task until success. This introduces
several important limitations. First, the agent acquires experience only
within a single task instance, and the resulting knowledge is not
transferred across tasks. Once a task has been solved, the agent must
repeat the full reflection process from scratch when encountering a new
task. This is inherently inefficient, since insights from one task could
often generalise to similar tasks (e.g., “in maze-solving tasks, avoid
revisiting the same path”). Under the current paradigm, however, the
agent is forced to relearn such lessons for each task. Second, in many
real-world settings, repeating the exact same task is not possible. For
example, in a game of chess one cannot require an opponent to reproduce
the same sequence of moves, and in a cooking scenario a mistake may
irreversibly consume the available ingredients.

Although the ability to learn online from experience across tasks is
highly desirable, it remains unclear whether self-reflection mechanisms
can produce reflections that generalise well enough to improve
performance on previously unseen tasks. We therefore ask the following
research question: Can LLMs be trained to generate self-reflections that
facilitate cross-task self-improvement, and if so, how?.

![Refer to caption](2605.20477v1/figures/ICT.png)

Figure 1: The In-context Training (ICT) task. In each turn, the
reflector model generates a new system prompt $`sp_{i}`$ based on the
previous performance of the actor model. The actor then interacts with a
batch of unseen tasks using the newly generated prompt. The quality of
the prompt is subsequently evaluated on a fixed held-out set of tasks.
In our experiments, we fine-tune the reflector while keeping the actor
model frozen.

To address this, we first define the In-context Training (ICT) task, a
framework for evaluating the ability of LLMs to learn from experience
for cross-task self-improvement (see
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")).
The ICT task implements a simple self-learning loop through a dual-LLM
design. The first model is the actor, which serves as the operational
agent interacting with external environments according to a system
prompt. Crucially, at each turn of the ICT task, the actor faces a new
unseen batch of tasks and has only one chance to solve each task. The
second model is the reflector, which evaluates the actor’s performance
and proposes an improved system prompt for the the next turn. The goal
of the reflector is to learn from the actor’s collected experiences in
order to generate a system prompt that generalises across tasks within a
given family of tasks. For example, in a maze-solving task, the
reflector should learn from previously encountered mazes in order to
produce a system prompt that enables the actor to solve any unseen maze
drawn from the same task family in a single attempt.

Next, we demonstrate that the ability to learn from experience is itself
a learnable skill by introducing a fine-tuning pipeline to train an LLM
to generate reflections that facilitate cross-task self-improvement. We
train a reflector to analyse a given system prompt alongside experiences
collected under that prompt, and to generate an improved system prompt
for future unseen tasks. Our method does not rely on human-provided
examples.

We evaluate our approach on ALFWorld \[[15](#bib.bib19)\] and
MiniHack \[[9](#bib.bib20)\], two benchmarks comprising diverse
interactive environments. Using these benchmarks within the ICT
framework, we show that a reflector trained on a set of task types can
generalise and improve performance on previously unseen task types using
only a small number of gathered experiences. We also show that, in some
cases, the model generalises beyond the benchmark on which it was
trained, transferring to substantially different environments.

Finally, we introduce MetaGym, a generic Python library for constructing
gym-like meta-environments from any gym-like
environment \[[2](#bib.bib16)\]. We release MetaGym as a tool to support
future research on self-improvement in LLM agents within the ICT
framework and beyond
([https://github.com/yuvalshalev1/MetaGym](https://github.com/yuvalshalev1/MetaGym)).

Our contributions can be summarised as follows:

1.  1.  A training pipeline for learning reflection strategies for
        cross-task self-improvement without reliance on human-provided
        labels.
2.  2.  The In-context Training task, a framework for evaluating online
        self-improvement of LLMs that generalises across task instances.
3.  3.  MetaGym, a Python library for constructing meta-environments from
        Gym-like environments.

## 2 Related Work

Prompt Optimisation. Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of
LLMs for prompt optimisation in static tasks \[[20](#bib.bib22),
[4](#bib.bib23), [1](#bib.bib24)\]. [Yang et al. \[20\]](#bib.bib22)
optimise prompts for mathematical reasoning and question answering using
closed-source LLMs, and [Choi et al. \[4\]](#bib.bib23) propose a
bi-level framework that jointly optimises task-specific user prompts and
a cross-task system prompt. In both cases, the optimiser observes only
final outputs or aggregate accuracy, not how its prompts shaped the
model’s behaviour during problem solving. In our setting, however, the
optimiser observes full interaction trajectories, enabling us to study
its ability to learn from the agent’s behaviour. [Agrawal et al.
\[1\]](#bib.bib24) leverage full reasoning trajectories to optimise
prompts through iterative updates to a prompt pool. However, their
scoring procedure relies on evaluating multiple candidate prompts on the
same batch of task instances. In contrast, our setting assumes that each
task is encountered only once and learning must occur online from
non-repeatable experience. More broadly, these works optimise prompts
using external procedure rather than fine-tuning the optimiser itself,
leaving open whether LLMs can be trained to learn better optimisation
strategies.

Prompt Optimisation for LLM-Agents. Recent work has explored prompt
optimisation for LLM agents in interactive environments, while
transferring experience across tasks \[[10](#bib.bib2),
[24](#bib.bib5)\]. [Sarukkai et al. \[10\]](#bib.bib2) maintain an
external database of self-generated successful trajectories and retrieve
similar examples as in-context demonstrations for the actor. This method
relies on embedding raw past trajectories directly into the prompt,
rather than consolidating them into a structured representation.
However, prior work shows that in-context demonstrations are not always
effective, even when produced by human experts \[[8](#bib.bib3)\]. [Zhao
et al. \[24\]](#bib.bib5) similarly rely on an external mechanism,
extracting “insights” from pairs of past experiences and maintaining
them through a voting procedure, before combining them with selected raw
experiences to construct task-specific prompts during inference time.
These methods therefore transfer experience through external memory and
retrieval, but leave open the question of whether an LLM can be trained
to learn reusable reflective strategies for cross-task self-improvement.

Reflection for Self-Correction. [Shinn et al. \[14\]](#bib.bib4)
introduce reflection for LLM agents as a feedback loop in which an agent
analyses its behaviour after failing a task and uses this analysis to
guide subsequent attempts. Since then, several works have explored how
to train LLMs to reflect more effectively in interactive environments.
[Yao et al. \[22\]](#bib.bib12), [Ge et al. \[6\]](#bib.bib14) and [Feng
et al. \[5\]](#bib.bib13) use dual-LLM architecture that separates actor
and reflector, with the former training only the reflector and the
latter training both components jointly using a gradient policy. Most
recently, [Jiang et al. \[7\]](#bib.bib15) proposed a meta-RL framework
in which a single LLM acts as both actor and reflector. However, all of
these methods focus on self-correction through repeated attempts at the
same task. They, therefore, leave open whether reflection can support
cross-task improvement by extracting reusable lessons from experience.

## 3 The In-context Training Task

Here, we introduce the In-context Training (ICT) task, a framework for
evaluating whether large language models can learn from experience to
achieve cross-task self-improvement. ICT is designed to capture a
realistic setting in which the same task cannot be repeated, and the
only opportunity for improvement lies in future tasks. The framework is
intentionally minimalistic, aiming to measure the model’s intrinsic
learning ability rather than optimise performance through external
machinery.

0:  $`\text{LLM}_{\text{refl}}`$, $`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$,
$`E^{\text{train}}`$, $`E^{\text{val}}`$, batch size $`k`$, meta-turns
$`N`$, initial system prompt $`sp_{0}`$

1:  $`sp^{*}\leftarrow sp_{0}`$, $`\quad score^{*}\leftarrow 0`$

2:  Sample $`\{e^{(0)}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{k}\sim E^{\text{train}}`$

3:
 $`obs_{0}\leftarrow\bigl\{\tau^{(0)}_{j}\sim\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}(e^{(0)}_{j};\,sp_{0})\bigr\}_{j=1}^{k}`$

4:  for meta-turn $`i=1,\dots,N`$ do

5:   Generate new system prompt
$`sp_{i}\sim\text{LLM}_{\text{refl}}(sp_{i-1},obs_{i-1})`$

6:
  $`score_{i}\leftarrow\sum_{e\in E^{\text{val}}}R(\text{LLM}_{\text{act}},e,sp_{i})`$

7:   if $`score_{i}>score^{*}`$ then

8:    $`sp^{*}\leftarrow sp_{i}`$,
$`\quad score^{*}\leftarrow score_{i}`$

9:   end if

10:   Sample $`\{e^{(i)}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{k}\sim E^{\text{train}}`$

11:
  $`obs_{i}\leftarrow\bigl\{\tau^{(i)}_{j}\sim\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}(e^{(i)}_{j};\,sp_{i})\bigr\}_{j=1}^{k}`$

12:  end for

13:  return $`sp^{*}`$

Algorithm 1 In-context Training (ICT)

The full process is formulated in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In 3 The In-context Training Task ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")
and illustrated in
[Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience").
We first define the reflector model (denoted
$`\text{LLM}_{\text{refl}}`$), whose learning capabilities we aim to
evaluate, the actor model (denoted $`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$), whose
policy we aim to optimise, and a class of tasks $`E`$ on which training
is performed. The task class is partitioned into a training set
$`E^{\text{train}}`$ and a validation set $`E^{\text{val}}`$. The
objective is for the tested $`\text{LLM}_{\text{refl}}`$ to analyse
episodes sampled from $`E^{\text{train}}`$ using
$`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$ and generate a system prompt $`sp`$ that
enables the actor $`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$ to perform effectively
across all tasks in $`E^{\text{val}}`$.

Formally, the objective of the reflector $`\text{LLM}_{\text{refl}}`$ is
to generate a system prompt $`sp^{*}`$ that maximises the cumulative
reward obtained by the actor across the validation tasks:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
sp^{*}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{sp}\sum_{i=1}^{|E^{val}|}R(\text{LLM}_{\text{act}},e_{i},sp)
``` |  | (1) |

where $`R(\text{LLM}_{\text{act}},e_{i},sp)`$ denotes the reward
obtained by the actor $`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$ on task
$`e_{i}\in E^{val}`$ when conditioned on the system prompt $`sp`$.

The reflector $`\text{LLM}_{\text{refl}}`$ is modelled as a meta-agent
interacting with a meta-environment. The meta-environment is initialised
with an initial system prompt $`sp_{0}`$ and samples a batch of $`k`$
tasks from the training set $`E^{\text{train}}`$. The meta-environment
then executes a batch of episodes using $`sp_{0}`$ and returns a
meta-observation $`obs_{0}`$, the full sequences of interactions between
the actor $`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$ and the sampled environments (line
3 of
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In 3 The In-context Training Task ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")).
Then, the meta-loop begins: at each meta-turn $`i`$, the reflector
$`\text{LLM}_{\text{refl}}`$ is prompted to generate a new system prompt
$`sp_{i}`$, conditioned on the previous system prompt $`sp_{i-1}`$ and
the last meta-observation $`obs_{i-1}`$ (line 5):

|     |                                                        |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       sp_{i}\sim\text{LLM}_{\text{refl}}(sp_{i-1},obs_{i-1})
       ```                                                     |     | (2) |

where $`obs_{i}`$ is the meta-observation consisting of the batch of
trajectories collected under $`sp_{i}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
obs_{i}=\{\tau^{(i)}_{j}\sim\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}(e^{(i)}_{j},sp_{i})\}_{j=1}^{k}
``` |  | (3) |

and $`\tau^{(i)}_{j}=(a_{0},o_{0},a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{T},o_{T})`$ is
the trajectory of actions $`a_{t}`$ and environment observations
$`o_{t}`$ produced by $`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$ on task
$`e^{(i)}_{j}`$ under system prompt $`sp_{i}`$.

The proposed system prompt $`sp_{i}`$ is then evaluated on the
validation tasks $`E^{\text{val}}`$, and sent to the meta-environment to
execute the next batch of episodes (lines 10-11).

## 4 Training LLMs to Learn from Experience

We now introduce our pipeline for fine-tuning LLMs to generate
reflections that facilitate cross-task self-improvement.

Dataset Creation. To construct the training dataset, we run the ICT loop
$`r`$ times for $`N`$ turns each, using a base model. At the end of each
turn $`i`$, we record the tuple
$`(sp_{i},obs_{i},e^{(i)}_{0},\dots,e^{(i)}_{k-1})`$, consisting of the
current system prompt $`sp_{i}`$, the meta-observation $`obs_{i}`$, and
the batch of tasks $`e^{(i)}_{0},\dots,e^{(i)}_{k-1}`$ used in that
turn. Repeating this process yields a fixed dataset $`\mathcal{D}`$ of
$`r\times N`$ data points in total. The motivation is to capture a
diverse set of system prompts arising from different stages of the ICT
process, which correspond to varying degrees of required improvement.
For example, if the reflector receives a system prompt that succeeds on
one task in the batch but fails on the others, it should be able to
analyse the factors that contributed to the successful case and
generalise them to the remaining tasks. Conversely, if the reflector
receives a system prompt that succeeds on all tasks in the batch, it
should generate a new system prompt that remains highly similar to the
previous one, potentially reproducing it exactly.

Reward Signal. As described in
[Equation 2](#S3.E2 "In 3 The In-context Training Task ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience"),
the reflector generates a system prompt $`sp_{i}`$ conditioned on the
previous system prompt $`sp_{i-1}`$ and the last batch of trajectories
$`obs_{i-1}`$ collected by $`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$ under
$`sp_{i-1}`$. Its immediate task is therefore to analyse how the
previous system prompt led to the actor’s observed performance on the
previous batch $`e^{(i-1)}`$, and to improve the prompt in light of the
issues revealed by those trajectories. Put differently, although the
reflector’s goal is to improve performance on future unseen tasks, its
intermediate objective is to answer the following question: “If I had
the opportunity to try the same batch of tasks again, what would I do
differently to improve my performance?”.

To encourage the model to account for observed performance issues and
incorporate corresponding fixes into the new system prompt, we derive
the training reward directly from the previous batch of tasks.
Specifically, the reward used to rank $`sp_{i}`$ is the average reward
obtained by the actor $`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$ on the batch
$`e^{(i-1)}`$ when conditioned on $`sp_{i}`$, that is, by replaying the
previous batch under the new system prompt $`sp_{i}`$. Formally, the
reward function is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}(sp_{i})=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}R(\text{LLM}_{\text{act}},\,e^{(i-1)}_{j},\,sp_{i}).
``` |  | (4) |

Notably, although the reward signal is derived from the previous batch
of tasks, the reflector should be explicitly prompted to analyse those
performance issues and generate a system prompt intended for future
tasks. This is essential to discourage in-context overfitting to the
most recently observed batch.

Training Procedure. We follow a standard training procedure for RL-based
fine-tuning, where in each training step, we sample a batch of tuples
$`(sp_{i},obs_{i},e^{(i)}_{0},\dots,e^{(i)}_{k-1})`$ from the
dataset $`\mathcal{D}`$ and update the parameters of
$`\text{LLM}_{\text{refl}}`$ using GRPO \[[12](#bib.bib17)\]. The
procedure is illustrated in
[Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In 4 Training LLMs to Learn from Experience ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience"):
for each tuple, the reflector samples a group of $`G`$ candidate system
prompts
$`\{sp^{(1)},\dots,sp^{(G)}\}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid sp_{i},obs_{i})`$,
and each candidate is scored using $`\mathcal{R}`$ as defined in
[Equation 4](#S4.E4 "In 4 Training LLMs to Learn from Experience ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience").
The scores are computed dynamically during training by executing the
batch of tasks $`e^{(i)}_{0},\dots,e^{(i)}_{k-1}`$ with
$`\text{LLM}_{\text{act}}`$ under each candidate system prompt.

![Refer to caption](2605.20477v1/figures/training_procedure.png)

Figure 2: A single training step illustrated on an ALFWorld-Cool and
Place example. A system prompt and its associated episode batch are
sampled from the dataset and fed into the reflector, which generates
multiple candidate system prompts. Each candidate is scored by replaying
the same tasks with the frozen actor, and the resulting scores drive
advantage estimation and parameter updates via GRPO.

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

All our experiments were conducted using the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
model \[[19](#bib.bib18)\] and the verl framework \[[13](#bib.bib21)\]
for RL-based fine-tuning. The datasets were constructed as described in
[Section 4](#S4 "4 Training LLMs to Learn from Experience ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience"),
using $`r=128`$ ICT loops of $`N=4`$ turns each, with
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct serving as both the actor model and the base
reflector model. For each benchmark, we trained two reflectors: one with
batch size $`k=3`$ and another with batch size $`k=5`$. The reflection
prompts used in our experiment are detailed in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Reflector Prompt ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience").
Training hyperparameters and compute resources are reported in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Compute and Training Details ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience").

MetaGym. Task execution for both the ICT loop and the fine-tuning
procedure is managed by MetaGym, our library for meta-environment
construction for LLM-agentic tasks. MetaGym instantiates an interactive
meta-environment in which each meta-action is represented by a system
prompt, and each returned meta-observation is a batch of rollouts
generated by an actor. Internally, it spawns task instances and executes
them in parallel. See
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C MetaGym ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")
for more details and a usage example.

Task Partitioning. The objective of the proposed training approach is to
train a reflector that performs effectively on the ICT task, where the
goal is to generate a general system prompt that achieves strong
performance across tasks within a given task type. A straightforward
evaluation strategy would be to divide task instances into training and
validation sets. However, this is insufficient: a reflector trained on
one task type could simply memorise a high-performing prompt for that
type and reproduce it at test time, thereby bypassing the in-context
reasoning the model is intended to learn. To mitigate this, we partition
tasks by type rather than by instance, yielding disjoint meta-train and
meta-test sets, each comprising distinct task types. Each task type
consists of a collection of similar tasks, from which the reflector is
expected to extract transferable insights that generalise to other tasks
within the same type. During training, the reflector is exposed
exclusively to task types from the meta-train set. At evaluation time,
it is required to generalise to previously unseen task types in the
meta-test set, generating reflections based solely on in-context
observations available at inference time.

#### 5.1.1 Environments

To construct the meta-train and meta-test sets, we use agentic benchmark
environments that could be partitioned into distinct task types.
Specifically, we use ALFWorld \[[15](#bib.bib19)\] and a subset of
MiniHack \[[9](#bib.bib20)\]. For each benchmark, we train a dedicated
reflector on the tasks in the corresponding meta-train set, and then
evaluate it on tasks drawn from the meta-test set of the same benchmark.

ALFWorld. ALFWorld is a benchmark comprising six task types, all set in
a partially observable, house-like textual environment. Following [Jiang
et al. \[7\]](#bib.bib15), we use Pick and Place, Examine in Light,
Clean and Place, and Heat and Place as the meta-train set, and Cool and
Place and Pick Two and Place as the meta-test set. For dataset creation,
we execute the ICT loop 32 times for each of the four meta-train task
types. Further details are provided in
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D ALFWorld Details ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience").

MiniHack. MiniHack is a benchmark comprising many tasks in
two-dimensional grid world environments. To construct a meta-set with
different task types, we use a collection of eight 5x5 grid world
environments. We use MiniHack-Room-Random-5x5-v0, MiniHack-Eat-v0,
MiniHack-Wield-v0, and MiniHack-Wear-v0 as the meta-train set, and
MiniHack-PutOn-v0, MiniHack-Zap-v0, MiniHack-Read-v0, and
MiniHack-Room-Dark-5x5-v0 as the meta-test set. For dataset creation, we
execute the ICT loop 32 times for each of the four meta-train task
types. Further details are provided in
[Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E MiniHack Details ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience").

### 5.2 Results

We evaluate the reflectors trained on ALFWorld and MiniHack on their
respective held-out meta-test sets. The ALFWorld reflectors are
evaluated using the Cool and Place and Pick Two task types, and the
MiniHack reflectors were evaluated on the Dark, Read, PutOn, and Zap
task types. Each reflector is tested using the same batch size it is
trained on. For each reflector and task type, we run the ICT task 10
times for 10 turns each. This repetition is designed to control for
noise introduced by model temperature and to evaluate robustness across
different in-context training tasks. Each run is initialised using a
different random seed to obtain different task batches, while the
validation sets are kept fixed across all runs. For each run, we select
the best-performing prompt, and the average success rates across the
winning prompts are summarised in
[Table 1](#S5.T1 "In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience"),
along with the performance of the untrained Qwen2.5-7-Instruct model and
the average result achieved using the initial prompt. For calculating
the average result of the initial prompt, we use the initial outcomes
from all runs across all four reflectors ($`n=40`$).
[Figure 3](#S5.F3 "In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")
shows representative examples of reflector outputs on the MiniHack-Read
and ALFWorld Cool and Place tasks. Below we discuss our findings.

|  |  | $`k=3`$ |  | $`k=5`$ |  |
| Environment | Initial prompt | Qwen2.5-7B | Trained (ours) | Qwen2.5-7B | Trained (ours) |

(Top) The reflector correctly deduces that the goal of MiniHack-Read

LLMs Can Be Trained to Achieve Cross-Task Self-Improvement.
[Table 1](#S5.T1 "In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")
reveals that across nearly all evaluated tasks and environments, our
trained reflector consistently outperforms the untrained
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct baseline, demonstrating that the ability to learn
from experience is itself a learnable capability. Reflectors trained on
one set of task types successfully transfer their improved reflection
ability to unseen tasks types – providing direct evidence that learning
from experience is itself a learnable meta-skill. The one exception is
the Zap task in MiniHack for the $`k{=}3`$ condition, which is the
hardest task and may require larger batches to meaningfully learn from.
Notably, our results indicate that untrained Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct was
also able to improve the initial system prompt when conditioned on
sampled episodes of the actor, suggesting that the ability to extract
reusable lessons from experience already exists in the model to some
extent.

More Meta-Turns Lead to Better Performance.
[Figure 4](#S5.F4 "In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")
presents the average best win rate achieved up to each turn, aggregated
across all tasks for each experimental group. Performance improves
consistently with additional meta-turns across all four groups and,
crucially, continues to increase beyond turn 4, the boundary of our
training data. This is an important finding: during training, our model
was exposed to prompts created only by the first 4 turns of the ICT
loop, yet at test time, it was able to recursively improve its own
generated prompts further beyond this horizon. In the ALFWorld
experiments, 55% ($`k{=}3`$) and 45% ($`k{=}5`$) of the best-performing
prompts were achieved after turn 4, while in the MiniHack experiments,
32.5% ($`k{=}3`$) and 37.5% ($`k{=}5`$) emerged after turn 4. Notably,
25% of the best ALFWorld $`k{=}3`$ prompts were not attained until
turn 10, suggesting that further meta-turns may yield additional
improvements.

(a) ALFWorld

![Refer to

(b) MiniHack

Figure 4: Average winning prompt success rate up to each turn,
aggregated across all tasks for each reflector. Shaded regions indicate
standard deviation across all random seeds. The dashed vertical line
marks turn 4, the end of the training horizon. Performance continues to
improve beyond the number of steps seen during training.

Effect of Batch Size. The batch size plays two important roles that can
influence the performance of the reflector. First, it determines the
number of episodes observed by the reflector in each turn, thereby
affecting the diversity of experiences from which it can learn. Notably,
when a task is difficult, a small batch size may contain no successful
episodes, making it more challenging for the reflector to extract useful
lessons in the absence of positive examples. Second, batch size affects
the fine-tuning process of the reflector itself: during training, if
none of the generated candidate prompts is successful on any of the
replayed tasks, the GRPO algorithm cannot compute advantages because all
rewards are zero. A larger batch size increases the likelihood of
obtaining a positive reward signal, particularly when tasks are
difficult and rewards are sparse.

Increasing the reflection batch size from $`k{=}3`$ to $`k{=}5`$ shows
different effects across the benchmarks (see
[Table 1](#S5.T1 "In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")
and
[Figure 4](#S5.F4 "In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")).
In ALFWorld, performance is similar across batch sizes, suggesting that
the quality of individual reflections remains largely unchanged. Taking
into account the total number of tasks experienced, $`k{=}3`$ shows a
clear advantage, as adding more episodes appears to be redundant while
costing more solving attempts. In MiniHack, the performance of the
$`k{=}5`$ reflector was, in most cases, better than that of the
$`k{=}3`$ reflector, suggesting that using larger batches can be more
effective for fine-tuning the reflector.

The untrained Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct performs worse under the $`k{=}5`$
condition across almost all tasks. Notably, in the Pick Two task, the
prompts it discovers show performance remaining close to the initial
prompt. One possible explanation is that processing five episodes
simultaneously presents a workload that is too high for Qwen2.5-7B to
handle effectively. One interesting exception is the Zap task in
MiniHack, where Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct performs better in the k=5
condition, which we attribute to the difficulty of the task.

Cross-Benchmark Generalisation. To test whether the meta-skill learned
by our method generalises beyond the training benchmark, we evaluate
reflectors trained only on MiniHack within ALFWorld. Results are shown
in
[Table 2](#S5.T2 "In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience"),
alongside the initial prompt and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct baselines. The
reflector trained on MiniHack with a batch size of $`k{=}5`$ outperforms
the untrained Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct baseline on 4 out of 6 tasks, while
achieving comparable performance on the remaining two. Notably, on both
the Examine in the Light and Heat and Place tasks, it outperforms
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct even under the $`k{=}3`$ condition, which we
previously observed in
[Table 1](#S5.T1 "In 5.2 Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")
to be easier within ALFWorld. This is a significant finding, as it
demonstrates transferability between fundamentally different benchmarks.
By contrast, the $`k{=}3`$ reflector does not achieve improved
performance and, in some cases, performs worse than the untrained model.
We attribute this, as discussed earlier, to more difficult training at
smaller batch sizes, where the reward signal is sparser.

### 5.3 Limitations

In our experiments, we trained only the reflector model in order to
isolate the contribution of prompt evolution to actor performance.
However, maintaining separate actor and reflector models is
computationally expensive in practice, as it requires holding two models
in memory simultaneously. Training a single model to serve both roles
could yield further performance gains.

During the ICT loop, we used a fixed held-out task set to identify the
best-performing prompt at the end of each loop. In real-world settings,
such a repeatable evaluation set may not be available, necessitating
alternative mechanisms for determining when to stop adaptation. One such
alternative is lifelong learning – continuously updating the system
prompt without a fixed stopping criterion – though this raises open
questions about the long-term stability of the generated prompts, which
we leave for future work.

## 6 Conclusion

In this work, we investigated whether LLMs can learn from their own
experience in-context in the realistic setting of online learning. We
introduced the In-context Training (ICT) task as an framework for
evaluating cross-task self-improvement, in which an LLMs repeatedly
analyses batches of unseen episodes and generates system prompts
intended to improve performance across a task family. To train models
for this setting, we proposed an RL-based fine-tuning approach that
derives reward signals from replayed input tasks. Across held-out task
types, our trained reflectors consistently outperform an untrained
baseline, showing that leaning from experience is itself a learnable
capability.

We believe this has important implications for language agents. Our work
provides both an evaluation framework and a training methodology for
cross-task self-learning, a capability likely to matter for
general-purpose agents operating in open-ended environments. We hope it
shifts attention from reflection within a single task instance to
reflection across tasks. Because our approach requires no annotated
examples and applies directly to agentic benchmarks, it is readily
extensible. To support further research, we release MetaGym (see
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C MetaGym ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")),
a Python library for constructing meta-environments for LLM agentic
tasks.

## Appendix B Compute and Training Details

All experiments were conducted on a cluster node equipped with four
NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips, each with 96 GB of GPU memory.
Each reflector was trained for approximately 20 hours. Each ICT
evaluation experiment, consisting of 10 full ICT loops, took
approximately 2 node hours. In total, training and evaluation across all
experiments required approximately 168 node hours.

[Table 3](#A2.T3 "In Appendix B Compute and Training Details ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience")
lists the hyperparameters used to train the four reflectors. All runs
use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the base model, GRPO \[[12](#bib.bib17)\] as
the training algorithm, and the verl framework \[[13](#bib.bib21)\] for
RL-based fine-tuning. Parameters that differ across runs reflect the
longer in-context histories produced by different batch sizes $`k`$ and
different observation lengths in different benchmarks. The checkpoint
used for evaluation was selected based on validation performance.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Hyperparameter | ALFWorld $`k{=}3`$ | ALFWorld $`k{=}5`$ | MiniHack $`k{=}3`$ | MiniHack $`k{=}5`$ |
| Base model | Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct |  |  |  |
| Algorithm | GRPO |  |  |  |
| Learning rate | $`3\times 10^{-6}`$ |  |  |  |
| Train batch size | 16 |  |  |  |
| PPO mini-batch size | 16 |  |  |  |
| PPO epochs | 2 |  |  |  |
| Rollout samples ($`n`$) | 8 |  |  |  |
| KL loss coefficient | 0.001 |  |  |  |
| Max prompt length | 8192 | 8192 | 9216 | 10240 |
| Max response length | 2048 | 2048 | 2048 | 1024 |
| Rollout max model len | 10240 | 10240 | 11264 | 11264 |
| Checkpoint used | 160 | 120 | 70 | 60 |

## Appendix C MetaGym

MetaGym is a Python library designed to support prompt optimisation and
self-improvement research for LLM agents. It natively implements the ICT
task from the perspective of the reflector as a meta-agent. Each
meta-action is a system prompt, and each returned meta-observation is a
batch of rollouts generated by the actor conditioned on that prompt.
Internally, the meta-environment spawns a batch of task instances and
executes them in parallel using a chosen actor, providing native
infrastructure for running the ICT loop described in
[section 3](#S3 "3 The In-context Training Task ‣ Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience").
MetaGym wraps a Gym-compatible environment \[[2](#bib.bib16)\] inside a
Gym-like meta-environment and handles the parallel execution and
trajectory collection required by the ICT framework. In our experiments,
all task execution across ALFWorld and MiniHack was managed through
MetaGym. The library ships with built-in support for both benchmarks and
provides instructions for integrating new environments, with the aim of
supporting future research on prompt optimisation and self-improvement
in LLM agents. MetaGym is released publicly alongside this work at

## Appendix D ALFWorld Details

For the ICT loop, we use the built-in training and evaluation splits
provided by the ALFWorld benchmark. The reflector receives task batches
sampled from the training split, while the full validation split is used
for evaluation. Each episode is limited to 25 steps.

### D.1 Actor prompt

initial system prompt $`sp_{0}`$ is shared across all ALFWorld

## Appendix E MiniHack Details

MiniHack environments are procedurally generated, so task instances are
produced by sampling random seeds. The reflector receives task batches
sampled from a designated range of training seeds, while a fixed set of
32 seeds is held out and used consistently as the validation set for the
ICT loop. Each episode is limited to 25 steps, with the exception of the
$`k{=}5`$ training run, where this limit was reduced to 18 steps to keep
episode trajectories within the model’s context length.

MiniHack natively exposes a large number of actions, many of which are
irrelevant to the tasks in our benchmark. To reduce ambiguity and keep
the context concise, we always provide the actor with a curated list of
available actions that are suitable for our task set, rather than the
full action space.

### E.1 Actor prompt
````
